title: What Lies Beneath the API — Benjamin Cowen, Modal

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that SFT and RL fine-tuning is the natural destination for maturing AI products, directly matching post-training and continual learning. Modal is a developer platform for serverless compute and the fine-tuning guidance applies across general AI product verticals. The talk covers post-training methods (SFT, RL), evaluation as a prerequisite and signal, and serving of fine-tuned models. Assumes ML and production systems familiarity but frames implementation as accessible in 300 lines of Python. Recorded conference presentation on the AI Engineer channel. All six evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript.

summary: Ben Cowen, a forward-deployed ML engineer at Modal, observes that as AI applications mature and specialize, companies increasingly adopt fine-tuning to achieve better performance, lower costs, and customized behavior. He describes a model spectrum: at one end, frontier APIs enable rapid development but permit no customization beyond prompt engineering; at the other, full custom training demands dedicated clusters, infrastructure engineers, and deep stack ownership. A middle ground is emerging through serverless compute platforms and open-source libraries that provide algorithm-level control without cluster management overhead, preserving fast iteration cycles. Cowen cites industry evidence: Intercom reports beating their frontier API at one-fifth the cost through fine-tuning, Pinterest claims orders-of-magnitude improvements, and Decagon articulates the core motivation—frontier labs optimize models to win broadly, while companies need models that win at their specific business logic. He offers three signals that fine-tuning may be warranted: paying more for the API than customers pay you, evals that have plateaued, and latency or throughput requirements no shared endpoint can meet. He cautions that without collected data and mature evals, training is premature, echoing the decades-old adage of garbage in, garbage out. His central takeaway is that companies which have built agent harnesses and are already evaluating products have the foundational components for reinforcement learning training. Supervised fine-tuning and RL can each be implemented in approximately 300 lines of Python using open-source libraries. Modal customers have scaled to 50,000–100,000 sandboxes for RL rollouts. Serverless training also enables hyperparameter tuning via rapid fan-out and early termination. For serving, options include vLLM, SGLang, Triton Inference Server, or custom Python workflows on serverless platforms with auto-scaling. Cowen urges teams to start collecting data and developing evals now, anticipating fine-tuning relevance within six months to a year.

sections.title: Introduction and Pattern Observation
sections.summary: Cowen introduces himself as a forward-deployed ML engineer at Modal, a general-purpose serverless compute platform. He has worked with a wide range of AI applications and observes that as products mature, companies increasingly turn to fine-tuning for performance and cost gains.

sections.title: Model Spectrum and Frontier API Limitations
sections.summary: Describes the model spectrum from frontier APIs to custom training. Frontier APIs unlock rapid development but cannot be customized beyond prompt engineering. Startups winning enterprise contracts with specific latency, throughput, or custom-metric requirements find little ability to customize shared endpoints.

sections.title: Traditional Fine-Tuning Costs and the Emerging Middle Ground
sections.summary: Traditional fine-tuning requires large clusters, resource isolation, and infrastructure engineers, creating massive stack responsibility. A new type of cloud provider with serverless compute and open-source libraries offers a middle ground with algorithm control and fast iteration. Cites Intercom at 1/5 the cost, Pinterest at orders-of-magnitude improvement, and Decagon's framing of divergent goals between frontier labs and businesses.

sections.title: Signals for When to Fine-Tune
sections.summary: Cowen's hot take: it is a matter of time until any differentiated product becomes domain-specific. Three signals indicate fine-tuning is warranted: paying more for the API than customers pay you, plateaued evals, and latency or throughput requirements no shared endpoint can meet. Without collected data and mature evals, training is premature.

sections.title: You Already Have What You Need
sections.summary: Central takeaway: if you have built an agent harness and are collecting eval data, you already have the prerequisites for RL training. Modern open-source libraries eliminate the need for hand-computed gradients or infrastructure experts. Supervised fine-tuning can be done in 300 lines of Python, with code available on Modal's examples repository.

sections.title: RL at Scale, Serving, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Serverless training enables hyperparameter tuning via rapid container fan-out and early termination. RL is also accessible in approximately 300 lines of code. Modal's unified APIs for sandboxes and GPU containers support RL rollouts at massive scale, with customers reaching 50,000–100,000 sandboxes. Serving options include vLLM, SGLang, Triton, or custom Python workflows on serverless platforms. Cowen urges audiences to start preparing data and evals now, anticipating fine-tuning within 6–12 months.
